nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name:  Sailor's choice
Scientific Name:  Haemulon parra
Other Common Names: ronco blanco, boquilla both in Spanish.

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum:  Chordata
	Class:  Osteichthyes
	Order:  Perciformes
	Family:  Haemulidae

Other:	Reference for Scientific Name (Desmarest 1823)
	Reference for Classification (Robins et al.1991)
	Revision date approximate
	H. parrai  invalid - literature misspelling

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  The sailor's choice is marketed commercially in the Caribbean (Cervigon 1966).
Recreational:  The sailor's choice is primarily taken recreationally but was not listed as a target species by fisherman in a creel survey conducted by U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service in the southern Indian River Lagoon (Van Os et al. 1980 unpub. report).
Ecological Role:  The sailor's choice is one of the most abundant haemulids in the southern portion of the Indian River Lagoon (Christensen 1965; Gilmore 1977), second in abundance only to pigfish, Orthopristis chrysoptera (Gilmore 1988).  It is common regionally along inshore Atlantic reef formations (Christensen 1965; Gilmore 1977, 1988).  Juvenile populations undoubtedly serve as a food source for a variety of estuarine predators.
Indicator:  Early life history of the sailor's choice is directly associated with seagrass meadows and mangrove habitats (Gilmore 1977, 1988).  Reductions in populations will, therefore, be directly associated with seagrass and mangrove habitat loss.

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  The sailor's choice is found from the Bahamas and southeast Florida to Brazil including the West Indies and the coast of Central America to the southern Gulf of Mexico (Courtenay 1961; Bohlke and Chaplin 1968).  The range in Florida is from the Keys north to the southern Indian River Lagoon (Christensen 1965; Gilmore 1988).  It is absent from the west Florida shelf (Smith et al. 1975).
Within Study Area:   The sailor's choice is restricted to the southern portion of the Indian River Lagoon system south of 28 degrees north latitude and is the most abundant grunt in the Jupiter, Florida area (Christensen 1965; Gilmore 1988).
Life Mode:  The adult sailor's choice is principally a structure associated epibenthic predator found near inlets and reef structures (Longley and Hildebrand 1941; Christensen 1965; Randall 1967; Gilmore 1977, 1988).  Spawning produces pelagic eggs (Breder and Rosen 1966).  As juveniles, they are found in seagrass bed and mangrove fringe habitats (Gilmore 1988; unpub. data).
Mobility and Migration: Little information is available on this subject, however the differences in adult and juvenile habitat indicate a movement from estuarine seagrass/mangrove habitats to the ocean inlet and continental shelf reef habitats with maturity (Gilmore pers. obs).

nodes.title: Habitat Type
nodes.body:
The sailor's choice is a structure associate.
Juvenile: juveniles are found inshore in the mangrove fringe and seagrass flats, and sometimes in low salinity tributaries (Courtenay 1961; Christensen 1965; Herrema 1974; Gilmore 1977).  The largest sailor's choice collected by Gilmore in extensive collections in the Indian River Lagoon seagrass beds was a 100 mm juvenile (unpub. data).
Adult: adults are found around inlets and oyster bars, and from shore to the offshore reef edge.

nodes.title: Substrate
nodes.body: Young sailor's choice are found over sand and mud bottoms in freshwater tributaries, seagrass meadows, and marginal mangrove forests (Christensen 1965; Gilmore 1977, 1988).  Adults and juveniles also found over sand, shell, rock, and around coral and worm reefs (Longley and Hildebrand 1941; Christensen 1965; Herrema 1974).

nodes.title: Physical/Chemical
nodes.body:
Salinity: The sailor's choice has been found in salinities ranging from 4.5 to 37.9 ppt (Springer and McErlean 1962; Christensen 1965) and is the most euryhaline of the Haemulon found in the Indian River Lagoon system.  Juveniles seem to be better able to tolerate lower salinities (Christensen 1965).
Temperature: The temperature range reported 19.9-34.0 C (Springer and McErlean 1962; Christensen 1965).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode:  The sailor's choice is gonochoristic, oviparous; pelagic eggs fertilized externally (Breder and Rosen 1966).
Mating/Spawning: Christensen (1965) reported that this species was probably a spring spawner, perhaps in March and April.  Sailor's choice in breeding condition have been collected in waters off the St. Lucie nuclear power plant on Hutchinson Island in May (Herrema et al. 1985), however late larvae and early juveniles (10-20 mm) have been collected in the Indian River Lagoon in February, April, and June through August (Gilmore unpub. data).
Fecundity: No information

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Egg:  Pelagic (Breder and Rosen 1966)
Larvae:  Post flexion larva have a size range of 6 to 10 mm (Lindeman 1986).
Juvenile:  Specimens from 10 to 15 mm and up are considered juveniles (Lindeman 1986).
Adult:  Mature adults average slightly larger than 200 mm (Courtenay 1961) but may reach 400 mm (Robins et al. 1986).

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: The adult sailor's choice, as with others of this genus, feeds almost exclusively at night, at or near the bottom (Longley and Hildebrand 1941; Randall 1967).  Specimens collected in the Tortugas in the early morning had stomachs filled with algae, mollusks, annelids, and sand (Longley and Hildebrand 1941).  Randall (1967) found 21 specimens collected around Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands contained over 70% crustaceans by volume after excluding large amounts of sand, algae, and detritus.

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body: The sailor's choice is dependent on a series of habitats (seagrass, mangrove, rock, reef, and inlets) throughout its life cycle.  As an important part of these systems, their abundance can influence benthic and epibenthic invertebrate populations.  Juvenile populations undoubtedly serve as a food source for a variety of estuarine predators.
